/photos/HST/_DSC0054-Edit.jpg.title: Starlight on the Slabs
/photos/HST/_DSC0054-Edit.jpg.alt: Creek running over granite slabs in the Big Arroyo beneath a deep blue star-lit sky, Sequoia National Park.
/photos/HST/_DSC0054-Edit.jpg.story: This one took hours and three separate takes — a golden hour version, a blue hour version, and an astro version once it was properly dark. What survived is a time blend: the sky from the astro frame, the foreground and middle ground from blue hour, thirteen seconds at ISO 80 while there was still light enough to hold texture in the granite. Shoot the stars alone and the bottom half of the picture is just black.
/photos/HST/_DSC0054-Edit.jpg.location: Big Arroyo, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC0181.jpg.title: Waiting Out the Weather
/photos/HST/_DSC0181.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of two backpackers beside Guitar Lake below Mount Whitney with storm cloud building above.
/photos/HST/_DSC0181.jpg.story: Storm light is the one gift of a Sierra afternoon in July — hard directional sun beneath a heavy lid, and gone within minutes. Seventy millimetres compresses the cloud down onto the basin, and the two figures stay tiny at the waterline because that is the honest proportion of the place. Monochrome: the cloud had all of the drama and none of the colour worth keeping.
/photos/HST/_DSC0181.jpg.location: Guitar Lake, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC0221.jpg.title: Lenticulars at First Light
/photos/HST/_DSC0221.jpg.alt: Lenticular clouds over the Sierra crest at dawn, seen from high on Mount Whitney above the Great Western Divide.
/photos/HST/_DSC0221.jpg.story: The colour before sunrise is the good material up here — cool, soft, and finished the instant direct light touches the ridges. Lenticulars mean serious wind aloft, which is bad news for a climb and excellent news for a photograph. Sixty-three millimetres tightened it to the layers I wanted: dark ridge across the bottom, the crest still in shadow, and the whole sky working above it.

/photos/HST/_DSC0238-Edit.jpg.title: Rothko's Sierra
/photos/HST/_DSC0238-Edit.jpg.alt: Pink dawn light on snow-streaked Sierra peaks photographed at 172mm from high on Mount Whitney, California.
/photos/HST/_DSC0238-Edit.jpg.story: The title is the idea. At 172mm the ridges stop reading as mountains and become horizontal bands of colour stacked one on the next — about as close to a colour field as landscape photography gets. Long lenses do exactly that: they flatten distance into layers. Handheld at ISO 1000 and 1/640, because at that hour and that temperature a tripod was never going to happen.

/photos/HST/_DSC0263-Edit.jpg.title: Sunrise Through the Windows
/photos/HST/_DSC0263-Edit.jpg.alt: Sunrise rays through a granite window on the Mount Whitney Trail, looking east over the Owens Valley.
/photos/HST/_DSC0263-Edit.jpg.story: Shooting into a rising sun is normally how you make a bad photograph. The exception is enough haze in the air to turn the light into visible shafts, and there was a valley full of it. The granite does two jobs — it frames the opening, and it gives the lens something dark to sit against, which keeps flare manageable. Metered for the sky and let the rock fall to silhouette.

/photos/HST/_DSC0293.jpg.title: Down from Trail Crest
/photos/HST/_DSC0293.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of two hikers descending the switchbacks below Trail Crest above a lake, Mount Whitney.
/photos/HST/_DSC0293.jpg.story: Early side light down a long slope is the best thing that can happen to a mountain: it separates each ridge from the next and puts texture into ground that reads flat by noon. The two figures set the scale of the switchbacks — without them this is an abstract. Black and white because the low sun had already gone warm, and the warmth was pulling attention off the structure.

/photos/HST/_DSC9760-HDR-Edit.jpg.title: Arnica Under the Spires
/photos/HST/_DSC9760-HDR-Edit.jpg.alt: Yellow arnica flowers on granite below the spires of Rowell Tower and Serpent's Tooth, Hamilton Lakes, Sequoia.
/photos/HST/_DSC9760-HDR-Edit.jpg.story: A near-far composition lives or dies on how close you are willing to get. The 14mm went down almost into the arnica — close enough that depth of field became the whole problem, solved at f/11 with the focus set a third of the way in. The range between shaded petals and sunlit granite needed a bracket. Cloud did the rest; in clear midday light there is no picture here.
/photos/HST/_DSC9760-HDR-Edit.jpg.location: Hamilton Lakes, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC9765-HDR.jpg.title: Lower Hamilton
/photos/HST/_DSC9765-HDR.jpg.alt: Lower Hamilton Lake in a bowl of polished granite on the High Sierra Trail, Sequoia National Park, under building cloud.
/photos/HST/_DSC9765-HDR.jpg.story: Twenty past twelve is the hour most landscape photographers are asleep or eating, and usually they are right. Moving cloud saved it — every few minutes the sun went behind, the granite stopped blowing out and the pool turned from glare to green. I bracketed and waited for those windows. The rock handles the composition on its own here: the trail climbs in the same lines the water falls.
/photos/HST/_DSC9765-HDR.jpg.location: Hamilton Lakes, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC9825-Edit.jpg.title: Thirty Seconds
/photos/HST/_DSC9825-Edit.jpg.alt: Long exposure of Hamilton Lake at dusk with a bleached driftwood log in the foreground, Sequoia National Park.
/photos/HST/_DSC9825-Edit.jpg.story: I worked this one for an entire evening, waiting on cloud that would actually do something. The log was the reason to be there — bleached, half-sunk, pointing straight into the frame — so the tripod went into the water beside it and the 14mm went low. Thirty seconds at f/11 turned the surface to slate. The range between the bright sky and the shaded wood was well past what a single frame holds, so it is a blend of brackets.
/photos/HST/_DSC9825-Edit.jpg.location: Hamilton Lakes, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC9860.jpg.title: The Climb Out of Hamilton
/photos/HST/_DSC9860.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of a hiker on the blasted ledge trail cut into the headwall above Hamilton Lake, Sequoia.
/photos/HST/_DSC9860.jpg.story: Scale is the hardest thing to photograph in this range and the only dependable solution is a person. So the frame is built to be mostly wall, with the figure small, high, and standing in the one patch of light on the ledge. Black and white because the rock was already doing everything — in colour it is grey stone under a blue lid, and the eye has nowhere to go.
/photos/HST/_DSC9860.jpg.location: Hamilton Lakes, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC9957.jpg.title: The Life Of a Foxtail
/photos/HST/_DSC9957.jpg.alt: Backlit foxtail pine growing out of granite in the Big Arroyo, Sequoia National Park, photographed at 500mm.
/photos/HST/_DSC9957.jpg.story: Late sun raked the tree from behind, lighting the needles while the rock stayed in shadow — a separation that lasts about twenty minutes a day. At 500mm from across the basin the background compresses to a flat wash and everything competing simply falls outside the frame. Backlight at that focal length is unforgiving about flare, so I shaded the front element by hood and shot into it anyway.
/photos/HST/_DSC9957.jpg.location: Big Arroyo, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/HST/_DSC9970.jpg.title: Glaciated Ground
/photos/HST/_DSC9970.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of glacier-polished granite slabs and peaks in the Big Arroyo, Sequoia National Park.
/photos/HST/_DSC9970.jpg.story: A flat grey afternoon over bare, glacier-scoured rock — in colour it is worth nothing at all. Monochrome turns the slabs structural: fracture lines become leading lines, and the separation between polished stone and shadowed cracks carries what colour could not. I set the horizon high and gave the foreground two thirds of the frame, because here the ground is the subject and the peaks are only the backstop.
/photos/HST/_DSC9970.jpg.location: Big Arroyo, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC1510.jpg.title: First Crossing
/photos/JMT/_DSC1510.jpg.alt: Backpackers crossing a log bridge over Lone Pine Creek in morning forest light on the Mount Whitney Trail.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1510.jpg.story: Mile one of two hundred thirty-eight, and the pack never heavier — a full week of food and 35 pounds on the Whitney Portal scale an hour earlier. I hung back at the creek and let the group string out single file across the logs; one figure per log beam is the difference between a snapshot of friends and a picture about a trail. Shade this deep at 26mm needs patience, not settings.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1510.jpg.location: Mount Whitney Trail, John Muir Wilderness, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC1514.jpg.title: Through the Willows
/photos/JMT/_DSC1514.jpg.alt: Two backpackers walking a rock-lined path through willows below Outpost Camp, granite spires above, Mount Whitney Trail.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1514.jpg.story: The two figures are day hikers I met thirty minutes out of the Portal — we would climb, camp, and summit together before their trail ended and mine began. At 17mm the willow corridor does the work: green walls, a stone floor, and the spires stacked overhead in the same frame. The Whitney trail is usually shot from above, looking down at Consultation Lake; its bottom half is quietly gorgeous.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1514.jpg.location: Mount Whitney Trail, John Muir Wilderness, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC1529.jpg.title: Slab Country
/photos/JMT/_DSC1529.jpg.alt: Hikers ascending granite slabs beneath a pinnacled ridge and deep blue sky on the Mount Whitney Trail.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1529.jpg.story: Past Outpost Camp the forest quits and the mountain turns to stone staircases. This is honest midday light — no golden hour, no drama, just granite glare and a sky so dark blue it reads processed when it is simply altitude. I kept the hikers small under the ridge because that proportion, tiny people on enormous stone, is the actual sensation of climbing this trail with a week of food on your back.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1529.jpg.location: Mount Whitney Trail, John Muir Wilderness, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC1535-Edit.jpg.title: Mountain Pride
/photos/JMT/_DSC1535-Edit.jpg.alt: Pink wildflowers blooming beside a whitewater cascade among granite boulders on the Mount Whitney Trail.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1535-Edit.jpg.story: Mountain pride, if I have my wildflowers right — it grows straight out of the rock next to running water, in defiance of everything around it. I got the lens low and close so the blooms would sit against the white noise of the cascade instead of the busy talus. On a one-lens trip the 17mm end is your macro, your landscape, and your everything else; you learn to stand in the right place.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1535-Edit.jpg.location: Mount Whitney Trail, John Muir Wilderness, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC1554.jpg.title: Twelve Thousand
/photos/JMT/_DSC1554.jpg.alt: Backpackers relaxing beside tents among granite boulders at Trail Camp below Mount Whitney in the evening.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1554.jpg.story: Trail Camp, 12,000 feet, the evening before the summit. We got in early on purpose — altitude respects nothing but time, and the plan was a 3:30am start. I shot into the sinking sun and let it flare over the ridge, because the honest picture of this place is not a landscape: it is people sitting on rocks, eating early dinners, quietly negotiating with tomorrow.

/photos/JMT/_DSC1562.jpg.title: Facing the Wall
/photos/JMT/_DSC1562.jpg.alt: A hiker stands among boulders at dusk facing the moonlit east face of Mount Whitney from Trail Camp.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1562.jpg.story: Last light at Trail Camp, moon already up, and one of my companions just stood there a long time reading the wall we would climb in the dark. I did not ask him to pose. ISO 10,000, handheld, almost as much open as this old lens goes — grain everywhere, and I kept every bit of it. Some exposures you take because the moment is leaving and the tripod is forty feet away in the tent.

/photos/JMT/_DSC1581.jpg.title: First Fire
/photos/JMT/_DSC1581.jpg.alt: Dawn alpenglow on the pinnacles of Mount Whitney from the 99 switchbacks, a hiker on the talus trail below.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1581.jpg.story: We left Trail Camp between 3:30 and 4, and by five the headlamps were off and the needles caught fire. This is the entire argument for summiting Whitney from Trail Camp instead of the car: when the first light lands, you are standing at 13,000 feet inside it. Shot moving, handheld at 17mm, because on a climb like this the tripod stays strapped — you take the fifteen best minutes as they come.

/photos/JMT/_DSC1583.jpg.title: The Cables
/photos/JMT/_DSC1583.jpg.alt: Sunrise over Owens Valley from the icy cables section of the Mount Whitney Trail, hikers crossing old snow.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1583.jpg.story: The cables section, early July: a leftover snowbank with meltwater running over it and refreezing, the whole passage glazed. I crossed first — closer to a crawl than a walk — precisely so I could turn around and photograph my two companions coming through with the sun cresting the Inyos behind them. Some frames you compose; this one I earned on my hands and knees.

/photos/JMT/_DSC1616.jpg.title: The Highest Roof
/photos/JMT/_DSC1616.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of hikers among summit boulders beside the stone Smithsonian hut on Mount Whitney.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1616.jpg.story: The summit hut at 14,505 feet, mid-morning, day two of twenty-two. Everyone around me had finished something; I had 220 miles left, and standing there I started calling this spot mile zero. Monochrome because summit light at ten in the morning has no color worth keeping — but the shapes, the blocks and the little stone house on the roof of the lower 48, carry the whole story by themselves.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1616.jpg.location: Mount Whitney Summit, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC1636.jpg.title: The Other Side
/photos/JMT/_DSC1636.jpg.alt: Wildflowers above the Hitchcock Lakes with Guitar Lake in the distance, from the west slope of Mount Whitney.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1636.jpg.story: Descending the west side of Whitney, the crowds gone, the JMT properly begun. The far lake is Guitar — that evening's camp — with the Hitchcock Lakes stacked between. One lens teaches you a habit: when you cannot zoom to the view, you walk to the foreground. I knelt into the flowers until they anchored the bottom of the frame and let the lakes recede in order, near to far, like a table of contents for the afternoon.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1636.jpg.location: Hitchcock Lakes, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC1648.jpg.title: Guitar Strings
/photos/JMT/_DSC1648.jpg.alt: A small creek winding through alpine meadow toward Guitar Lake below Mount Whitney at golden hour.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1648.jpg.story: The inlet stream at Guitar Lake, camp within earshot, summit day finally over. A thirteenth of a second,  tripod-mounted, just enough to soften the water while the meadow grass stays sharp. After eleven hours on the mountain I had energy for exactly one composition, so I picked the one the landscape had already drawn: a bright line of water leading home.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1648.jpg.location: Guitar Lake, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC1804.jpg.title: Gathering Weather
/photos/JMT/_DSC1804.jpg.alt: Storm clouds building over tundra and tarns below Forester Pass on the John Muir Trail in the morning.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1804.jpg.story: Morning of the Forester day, and the sky already meant business. My only plan was to be off the pass and descending before noon, so this was shot on the move — 17mm, sky given two-thirds of the frame, because the sky was the story. Three weeks of cloudless postcard blue on this trail, and the one morning the weather showed up, it pointed itself at the highest pass on the route.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1804.jpg.location: Tyndall Creek Basin, Sequoia National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC1827.jpg.title: The Divide
/photos/JMT/_DSC1827.jpg.alt: Black and white panorama from Forester Pass at 13,120 feet over the lakes and peaks of upper Kings Canyon.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1827.jpg.story: The view from Forester Pass, highest point of the Pacific Crest Trail, held for about ninety seconds because the clouds behind me had a schedule. The north side below this was wall-to-wall snow with no visible trail — part of the descent happened on my feet, the rest on my ass, and by the bottom Forester had somehow become my favorite pass of the trip. Monochrome, because that sky in color was gray anyway; in black and white it is architecture.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1827.jpg.location: Forester Pass, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC1865.jpg.title: Iron Water
/photos/JMT/_DSC1865.jpg.alt: A dark tarn beneath the snow-streaked headwall on the north side of Forester Pass, Kings Canyon National Park.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1865.jpg.story: First miles down the north side of Forester, fresh off the snow slide, legs still shaking slightly. The tarn had barely melted out and the water was that heavy, lightless almost-black that only exists at 12,000 feet in early season. I exposed for the water, not the snow — let the highlights defend themselves — because the weight of it was the picture.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1865.jpg.location: Forester Pass, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC1878-Edit.jpg.title: Running Green
/photos/JMT/_DSC1878-Edit.jpg.alt: A meltwater creek running over green moss through a meadow below Forester Pass, Kings Canyon National Park.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1878-Edit.jpg.story: An unnamed creek in the meadows past Forester — after a morning of snow, rock, and iron-colored water, the sudden green felt almost loud. A sixth of a second at f/7.1 with the little tripod splayed at its full fifteen inches, which for once was exactly the right height: this is a composition that lives at boot level. The Sierra rations its color up high; you shoot it when it appears.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1878-Edit.jpg.location: Upper Bubbs Creek, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC1939.jpg.title: Before the Rain
/photos/JMT/_DSC1939.jpg.alt: Storm clouds over East Vidette and the Bubbs Creek forest, from the climb above Vidette Meadow.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1939.jpg.story: Shot on the climb out of Vidette Meadow with rain starting and thunder working somewhere behind the ridge. I was hunting a campsite — above the mosquitos, mindful of the very specific signs about local bears stealing entire canisters — and East Vidette kept appearing through the trees looking like this. Thirty minutes after the shutter, the sky opened. By morning the tent was sheathed in ice. Worth it.
/photos/JMT/_DSC1939.jpg.location: East Vidette, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC2021.jpg.title: Cloud Theater
/photos/JMT/_DSC2021.jpg.alt: Towering afternoon clouds over the Kearsarge basin with distant lakes far below, from near Kearsarge Pass.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2021.jpg.story: The Kearsarge resupply day: out of the wilderness, down 2,600 feet to a bear box at Onion Valley, then back up the same pass with five days of food. This was the consolation — a sky performing over the whole basin while I climbed under fresh weight. When the light is flat and midday, clouds are composition; I gave them most of the frame and kept the lakes as a footnote of scale.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2021.jpg.location: Kearsarge Pass, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC2074.jpg.title: Kiersarge Mirror
/photos/JMT/_DSC2074.jpg.alt: Fifteen-second dawn exposure of the Kearsarge Pinnacles reflected in a still Kearsarge Lake before sunrise.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2074.jpg.story: 4:55 in the morning at Kearsarge Lakes, a fifteen-second exposure in the blue before anything happens. This is the shot the knee-high tripod was born for — at shin height the near shore, the reflection, and the Pinnacles stack into one plane of glass. The day before had been the hardest of the trip: a frozen tent, a resupply hauled back over the pass. Mornings like this are how the ledger balances.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2074.jpg.location: Kearsarge Lakes, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC2137.jpg.title: The Cast
/photos/JMT/_DSC2137.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of a fly fisherman casting from a rock at Rae Lakes below Fin Dome in the evening.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2137.jpg.story: This is the first photograph I ever took of Robert, within an hour of meeting him. He was fishing beside the ford at Rae Lakes when I walked up and asked a stranger whether this was paradise and how to cross it; he answered both. A 1/1600th to freeze the loop of the line mid-air, and monochrome because the cast, the rock, and Fin Dome needed nothing else. We finished the trail together.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2137.jpg.location: Rae Lakes, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC2304.jpg.title: The Quiet Side
/photos/JMT/_DSC2304.jpg.alt: Evening in the rocky basin above Lake Marjorie near Pinchot Pass, Crater Mountain on the horizon.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2304.jpg.story: I took Pinchot Pass in the evening rather than saving it for morning like the guidebooks draw it, and camped alone in the barrens above Lake Marjorie. That is Crater Mountain across the basin. The color up here after sunset sits barely above monochrome — gray rock, violet air — and I kept it that way instead of warming it, because the whole point of an evening pass is arriving on the empty, quiet side of it.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2304.jpg.location: Lake Marjorie, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC2446.jpg.title: Gold Rush
/photos/JMT/_DSC2446.jpg.alt: Half-second exposure of a cascade in golden evening light at the Palisade Lakes below Mather Pass.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2446.jpg.story: Evening at the Palisade Lakes after crossing Mather, with the Golden Staircase waiting below camp for morning. A half-second exposure, no dark filter needed — my strongest ND was a 3-stop, so silky water on this trip meant simply waiting for the light to drop low enough. It usually did around the hour the light also turned to this. Constraints have a way of scheduling your best work for you.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2446.jpg.location: Palisade Lakes, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC2779.jpg.title: Meltwater
/photos/JMT/_DSC2779.jpg.alt: Two backpackers crossing a snowmelt creek below Muir Pass, snowfields on the peaks above.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2779.jpg.story: The climb to Muir Pass in early July is a plumbing system: every snowfield above you arrives in the trail somewhere below. I let the two hikers reach the middle of the crossing before the shutter — boots apart, poles planted, the exact geometry of everyone's morning up here. At 17mm the peaks stay in frame to explain where all this water keeps coming from.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2779.jpg.location: Muir Pass, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC2799.jpg.title: The Last Mile
/photos/JMT/_DSC2799.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of hikers on the barren rock approach to Muir Pass, Kings Canyon National Park.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2799.jpg.story: The final approach to Muir Pass, where the Sierra stops pretending to be hospitable — no trees, no meadow, just shattered rock and old snow to the horizon. I racked the lens to its long end, all of 35mm, to stack the walkers against the emptiness. In color this scene is brown and dispiriting; in black and white it becomes what it actually felt like, which is walking on another planet.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2799.jpg.location: Muir Pass, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC2810.jpg.title: Moonscape
/photos/JMT/_DSC2810.jpg.alt: Hikers in a vast basin of broken rock and snow patches near Muir Pass, black and white.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2810.jpg.story: Same climb, wider view, two people. Near Muir Pass the scale becomes difficult to photograph honestly — everything is enormous and nothing offers a reference, so a human scale has to do all the measuring. A 1/1600th of pure reflex; the figure walked into the one bright patch and the frame assembled itself. Days like this you are less a photographer than a lookout.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2810.jpg.location: Muir Pass, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC2813-HDR.jpg.title: The Window
/photos/JMT/_DSC2813-HDR.jpg.alt: View through the stone window of the Muir Hut over the barren lake country north of Muir Pass.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2813-HDR.jpg.story: The Muir Hut has stood on the pass since 1930, the only roof for a day's walk in any direction, and its window frames the country you are about to descend into. The interior stone sits many stops darker than the basin outside, so this is a bracketed exposure blended back together — the one technique this trip allowed itself. The only frame in my JMT gallery with walls in it.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2813-HDR.jpg.location: Muir Hut, Muir Pass, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC2848.jpg.title: Opposite Directions
/photos/JMT/_DSC2848.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of southbound hikers walking the barren shore of Wanda Lake toward Muir Pass.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2848.jpg.story: These hikers are southbound, a couple of miles from the hut, walking into the moonscape I was walking out of. Passing SOBOs late in your trip is a strange mirror — everything behind you is still ahead of them, and you can see it in the pace. Shot at 17mm across the full sweep of Wanda Lake, monochrome, because the encounter felt like a diagram: two lines crossing once.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2848.jpg.location: Wanda Lake, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC2907.jpg.title: Sapphire
/photos/JMT/_DSC2907.jpg.alt: Dark deep water of Sapphire Lake beneath a sheer granite wall in Evolution Basin, black and white.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2907.jpg.story: Sapphire Lake is named for its color, and I photographed it in black and white anyway — the depth reads better than the hue. That water is glacial, hundreds of feet of it in places, and against the wall it goes nearly black in a way blue never quite communicates. Descending Evolution Basin you pass a lake like this every hour and have to keep choosing which ones cost you daylight.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2907.jpg.location: Sapphire Lake, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC2975-HDR.jpg.title: The Reason
/photos/JMT/_DSC2975-HDR.jpg.alt: Sunset light over the waterfall at Evolution Lake’s outlet in Evolution Basin, Kings Canyon National Park.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2975-HDR.jpg.story: My tent stood twenty feet from this waterfall, on a ledge where Evolution Lake pours off the shelf — the best campsite of 238 miles, found at the end of a faint use path behind a hill. I shot straight into the falling sun, bracketed, and blended the exposures later. When people ask why anyone carries a tripod and a full-frame camera across the Sierra on foot, this frame is the shortest answer I have.
/photos/JMT/_DSC2975-HDR.jpg.location: Evolution Lake, Kings Canyon National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3065.jpg.title: Islands
/photos/JMT/_DSC3065.jpg.alt: Marie Lake’s island-dotted blue water from the Selden Pass trail at midday, John Muir Wilderness.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3065.jpg.story: Marie Lake from the Selden Pass side, shot at high noon — the hours photographers are taught to write off. Some subjects do not care: the lake is all shape, a scatter of islands that reads like a map of itself, and midday blue is its true color. At 28mm I framed it as geography rather than mood. Rule of thumb from three weeks out here: when the light is boring, look for places that are drawn well.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3065.jpg.location: Marie Lake, John Muir Wilderness, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3111.jpg.title: The Ferryman
/photos/JMT/_DSC3111.jpg.alt: Black and white photo aboard the Edison Queen ferry crossing Lake Edison, Captain Paint at the helm on the left.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3111.jpg.story: Captain Paint — Perry Harris — at the helm of the Edison Queen, carrying hikers to Vermilion Valley Resort the way he had for years. We spent an evening of our zero day drinking and trading stories with him. Six weeks after this frame, his ferry struck a rock; he steered it ashore, got every passenger off safely, and collapsed at the helm. He was 68. I am glad this photograph exists.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3111.jpg.location: Lake Thomas A. Edison, Sierra National Forest, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3151-HDR.jpg.title: Edison Blue
/photos/JMT/_DSC3151-HDR.jpg.alt: Long exposure of Lake Edison at night from Vermilion Valley Resort, mountains mirrored in still water.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3151-HDR.jpg.story: The dark end of the beach at VVR on my zero day, two and a half seconds of exposure at 35mm. A reservoir is not a wild lake and I did not try to pretend otherwise — the flatness, the strange stillness of managed water, is its own subject. After twelve days of alpine drama there was something restful about photographing a horizontal line and going to bed full of burger.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3151-HDR.jpg.location: Lake Thomas A. Edison, Sierra National Forest, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3155.jpg.title: Back to Work
/photos/JMT/_DSC3155.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of backpackers riding the morning ferry across Lake Edison back to the John Muir Trail.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3155.jpg.story: The morning ferry back to the trail is the quietest boat in California — everyone aboard is leaving showers, chairs, and cold drinks behind, and nobody talks. I shot from the bench at 17mm, close enough that the packs and hat brims do the storytelling. A companion piece to the crossing two days earlier: same boat, same lake, entirely different silence.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3155.jpg.location: Lake Thomas A. Edison, Sierra National Forest, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3166.jpg.title: Morning Commute
/photos/JMT/_DSC3166.jpg.alt: A backpacker climbing through sunlit lodgepole forest above Mono Creek toward Silver Pass.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3166.jpg.story: The climb out of Mono Creek after the zero day, legs relearning their job. Forest interiors are the hardest Sierra subject — chaos in every direction — until the morning sun cuts shafts through the lodgepoles and hands you an aisle. I waited for the figure to reach the lit gap. Auto ISO ran to 5600 in the shade and I let it; grain in the woods bothers no one, least of all the woods.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3166.jpg.location: Mono Creek, John Muir Wilderness, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3257.jpg.title: Reading the Light
/photos/JMT/_DSC3257.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of a backpacker standing above Lake Virginia watching the evening light develop.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3257.jpg.story: Robert above Lake Virginia, deciding whether the light was done. It was not — the red meadows an hour later made the evening — but I like this frame better than what followed: the pack still on, the lake going pewter, a person doing the same arithmetic I was doing. Photographing photographers- at-heart is the easiest portraiture there is. They hold still on their own.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3257.jpg.location: Lake Virginia, John Muir Wilderness, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3272-HDR.jpg.title: Virginia in July
/photos/JMT/_DSC3272-HDR.jpg.alt: Red meadow grasses and still water at Lake Virginia at dusk in the John Muir Wilderness.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3272-HDR.jpg.story: The meadows around Lake Virginia turn genuinely red in July, dusk light on wine-colored grass. This is a bracketed blend at 35mm to hold both the glowing meadow and the darkening sky, made about 7:30 in the evening at the softest camp of the trip. Silver Pass in the morning, Bart's last day with us in the middle, and this at the end of it.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3272-HDR.jpg.location: Lake Virginia, John Muir Wilderness, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3370.jpg.title: Small Ones Swim
/photos/JMT/_DSC3370.jpg.alt: A fisherman casting into Purple Lake in morning light while another hiker watches from the shore trees.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3370.jpg.story: Robert fishing Purple Lake in the morning, Ronda supervising from the trees. His system was fixed law by then: small fish swim, big fish meet the pan — he carried spices and oil the way I carried a tripod, a hundred grams of conviction. Two miles after this frame, at the Duck Pass junction, our group of four became three. Photographs from ordinary mornings appreciate fast on a trail.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3370.jpg.location: Purple Lake, John Muir Wilderness, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3446-Enhanced-NR.jpg.title: Above the Falls
/photos/JMT/_DSC3446-Enhanced-NR.jpg.alt: The Milky Way core over two backpacking tents at a wilderness camp above Rainbow Falls at night.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3446-Enhanced-NR.jpg.story: An off-trail camp above Rainbow Falls, no moon, and the galactic core standing straight up out of the trees. Fifteen seconds at f/3.2, ISO 1000 — the 440-gram tripod and the f/2.8 lens splitting the night shift between them. Three weeks of cloudless skies were a curse for sunsets and a gift for this: I could plan an astro camp days ahead with total confidence the stars would show up for work.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3446-Enhanced-NR.jpg.location: Rainbow Falls, Ansel Adams Wilderness, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3457.jpg.title: Organ Pipes
/photos/JMT/_DSC3457.jpg.alt: Black and white view up the columnar basalt cliff of Devils Postpile with a pine at the rim.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3457.jpg.story: Devils Postpile from directly below, 35mm aimed straight up the columns. The hexagonal jointing is so regular it photographs like architecture, so I treated it as architecture: monochrome, hard geometry, one pine at the rim for the organic counterargument. A ten-minute detour off the JMT the morning we dropped into Reds Meadow for burgers, ice cream, and the third resupply.

/photos/JMT/_DSC3592.jpg.title: Banner Day
/photos/JMT/_DSC3592.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of a hiker sitting on a rock gazing at Banner Peak across Thousand Island Lake.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3592.jpg.story: Arrival evening at Thousand Island Lake, the most photographed water on the John Muir Trail. Sometimes the icon is best shot by way of the people looking at it.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3592.jpg.location: Thousand Island Lake, Ansel Adams Wilderness, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3649-HDR.jpg.title: One in a Thousand
/photos/JMT/_DSC3649-HDR.jpg.alt: Six-second twilight exposure of Banner Peak over Thousand Island Lake with pink afterglow on the summit.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3649-HDR.jpg.story: Banner Peak at blue hour, six seconds of exposure smoothing Thousand Island Lake, the last pink hanging on the summit snow. Every JMT hiker makes a version of this picture; I waited for the hour when nobody else was standing at the shore and the lake had settled. Bracketed and blended for the sky. If this gallery has a single frame that explains why the trail is walked, I think it is this one.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3649-HDR.jpg.location: Thousand Island Lake, Ansel Adams Wilderness, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3751.jpg.title: Midday Break
/photos/JMT/_DSC3751.jpg.alt: Hikers resting beside the Lyell Fork in Tuolumne Meadows below granite domes, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3751.jpg.story: Shot from the bridge over the Lyell Fork, which is the only place you get this line of sight down the meadow. The picture is not really about the granite — it is about a group taking their break in the middle of the day, which is what most of a long day on this trail actually consists of. Middle of the day, middle of the hike, nothing dramatic happening.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3751.jpg.location: Lyell Fork, Tuolumne Meadows, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3788-Enhanced-NR.jpg.title: Oil Painting
/photos/JMT/_DSC3788-Enhanced-NR.jpg.alt: Cathedral Peak reflected in still water at sunset under textured cloud, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3788-Enhanced-NR.jpg.story: One of my favourites. Cathedral Peak and its reflection at sunset, and the light that evening did something I have not managed to repeat since — it reads more like an oil painting than a photograph. The cloud is doing at least half the work. Without that texture overhead the top of the frame would be empty and the reflection would have nothing to answer to.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3788-Enhanced-NR.jpg.location: Cathedral Peak, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3804-Edit.jpg.title: Into the Lupine
/photos/JMT/_DSC3804-Edit.jpg.alt: A field of lupine in bloom below Cathedral Peak, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3804-Edit.jpg.story: We were walking down towards the valley when this field stopped me — lupine in a quantity I had not expected, and very close to the violet the sky was already doing. I put the camera low, just under the flowers, and held focus on the peak rather than on them. The point was to place the viewer inside the field instead of looking at it from the edge.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3804-Edit.jpg.location: Cathedral Peak, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3832.jpg.title: The Detour
/photos/JMT/_DSC3832.jpg.alt: View from the Clouds Rest summit ridge over Half Dome and Yosemite Valley under summer clouds.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3832.jpg.story: We left the JMT on our longest day to go over the top of Clouds Rest, because finishing 238 miles without the best view in Yosemite felt like a technicality. From the summit ridge Half Dome sits below you — an angle that quietly rearranges your sense of the park — and the Valley is a trench full of light. At 24mm, with actual clouds for once, three weeks of walking laid out to the horizon.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3832.jpg.location: Clouds Rest, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC3921-HDR.jpg.title: Silver Dome
/photos/JMT/_DSC3921-HDR.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of Half Dome in evening haze from the Clouds Rest descent, Yosemite Valley beyond.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3921-HDR.jpg.story: Half Dome going silver in the evening haze, from the descent off Clouds Rest on our second-to-last day. The haze flattened every color to pastel, so I let the frame be about tone instead — bracketed, blended, and finished in black and white, the dome as a shape among receding shapes. After 230 miles the legs were spent, but light like this cancels fatigue for exactly as long as it lasts.
/photos/JMT/_DSC3921-HDR.jpg.location: Clouds Rest, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC4039.jpg.title: Half Gold
/photos/JMT/_DSC4039.jpg.alt: Half Dome catching last light above a meadow and the valley road, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/JMT/_DSC4039.jpg.story: This was after the trail rather than on it. We were wandering the valley with nothing much left to do, which is a strange state to be in when you have spent weeks walking towards somewhere, and this arrangement stopped me: road, meadow, trees, Half Dome, nothing else in it. Minimal to the point of being almost graphic. I did not have to work for this one at all.
/photos/JMT/_DSC4039.jpg.location: Half Dome, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/JMT/_DSC4063-Enhanced-NR.jpg.title: The Dry Mirror
/photos/JMT/_DSC4063-Enhanced-NR.jpg.alt: Star trails circling above Half Dome over the dry bed of Mirror Lake, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/JMT/_DSC4063-Enhanced-NR.jpg.story: The backpackers' camp sits close to Mirror Lake, so we walked over — and in the middle of July there was almost no lake there at all. We sat down in what should have been the bottom of it. Nine hundred seconds, with Half Dome above and what water was left in the foreground: long enough for the stars to draw their arcs instead of sitting still.
/photos/JMT/_DSC4063-Enhanced-NR.jpg.location: Mirror Lake, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/cities/_DSC5344.jpg.title: Enshrined Forever
/photos/cities/_DSC5344.jpg.alt: Long-exposure black-and-white photo of the Lincoln Memorial statue with constantly passing visitors
/photos/cities/_DSC5344.jpg.story: I set up inside the chamber, and with everyone too busy to notice me, I had time to work the shot. People streamed past the whole time, while Lincoln has sat there for decades — that contrast, the still monument against the flowing crowd, was the whole idea. I held a five-second exposure so the visitors blurred into ghosts while the statue stayed perfectly sharp.

/photos/cities/_DSC8037.jpg.title: Pacific Park After Dark
/photos/cities/_DSC8037.jpg.alt: Long-exposure night photo of Santa Monica Pier's lit Ferris wheel and roller coaster reflected on the wet beach.
/photos/cities/_DSC8037.jpg.story: I walked down onto the sand well after sunset, when the Pacific Wheel and the little roller coaster were the brightest things for miles. The idea was to let the tide do the work: a four-second exposure smeared the incoming surf into a soft sheen and stretched every pink and purple light into long ribbons across the wet beach. At f/8 the pier stayed crisp while the water turned to glass.
/photos/cities/_DSC8037.jpg.location: Santa Monica Pier, Santa Monica, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC5570.jpg.title: Bloom and Basin
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5570.jpg.alt: Desert gold wildflowers on a slope above the salt flats of Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5570.jpg.story: I made this on the way up rather than at the top. From down on the flat the two things never meet, but from the slope the flowers stack into verticals and the basin lays a hard horizontal in behind them, warm against cool. That is the entire picture. I kept the bloom close enough to the lens that it reads as texture instead of as a subject.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5570.jpg.location: Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC5599-Edit.jpg.title: False Frost
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5599-Edit.jpg.alt: Salt crust at Badwater Basin lit low across its ridges during blue hour, Death Valley National Park.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5599-Edit.jpg.story: One of my favourites, and the only frame here that isn't natural light. The camera went as low on the tripod as it would go — salt has no shape at all from standing height. Then a flash off the camera entirely, held out to one side, so the light rakes across the crust instead of flattening it. Blue hour gave me the sky; the flash gave the ground its edges.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5599-Edit.jpg.location: Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC5707.jpg.title: For Scale
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5707.jpg.alt: A lone figure silhouetted on a badlands ridge at sunrise under a pink and purple sky, Zabriskie Point, Death Valley.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5707.jpg.story: I was still hunting for a composition when someone walked up onto that hill. Everything I had tried until then failed for the same reason — nothing in the frame told you how big any of it was. They fixed that by existing. I shot it and walked away convinced I had come back with nothing, which turns out to be the least reliable feeling in photography.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5707.jpg.location: Zabriskie Point, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC5808.jpg.title: Wrong Colours
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5808.jpg.alt: Hikers on a ridge above the coloured badlands of Golden Canyon with the Panamint Range beyond, Death Valley.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5808.jpg.story: This is not the desert people picture, and it is not the mountains people picture either. The colours are wrong for both, which is exactly why I wanted it. The hikers on the ridge are walking out of the frame rather than into it, and that felt more honest about the scale of the place — you don't arrive somewhere like this, you cross it and keep going.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5808.jpg.location: Golden Canyon, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC5828.jpg.title: The Committee
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5828.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of four hikers silhouetted on the ridge of a dune at Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes, Death Valley.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5828.jpg.story: I was out scouting for sunset when this arranged itself above me: four people on the ridge, mid-argument about whether to keep climbing. One pointing, one very obviously finished. It reads like a single panel of a comic. I framed wide and let the dune take most of the picture, because the joke only works while they are still small enough to be figures rather than people.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5828.jpg.location: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC5865.jpg.title: Sand to Sky
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5865.jpg.alt: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes at blue hour, warm sand giving way to blue and pink sky over the distant salt basin.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5865.jpg.story: Sand holds the last of the warm light for a while after the sky above it has gone cold. That mismatch is the picture — a gradient running the full height of the frame, yellow at your feet, then blue, then pink out over the far basin. I composed around the transition itself rather than around any particular dune, which is why nothing here is the subject.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC5865.jpg.location: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC6007.jpg.title: Fallen Sky
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6007.jpg.alt: Clouds reflected in floodwater on the salt flats of Badwater Basin, the Panamint Range beyond, Death Valley.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6007.jpg.story: Second day of trying to make something work down here. The water changed it — a flooded basin stops being ground and becomes a mirror, and once the sky is underneath you as well as above you the whole thing goes abstract. The mountains end up as the only element still reading as itself. Everything else in the frame is cloud, twice over.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6007.jpg.location: Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC6068.jpg.title: Telescope Blue
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6068.jpg.alt: Telescope Peak above Badwater Basin at late blue hour, salt formations visible beneath standing water, Death Valley.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6068.jpg.story: Late blue hour, and salt does something strange with it. White crust throws back almost everything that lands on it, so the colour of the sky ends up spread across the entire basin instead of staying up where it belongs. Telescope Peak anchors the far side. The salt formations still readable under the water are what keep this from tipping over into looking invented.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6068.jpg.location: Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC6099.jpg.title: Badwater Fire
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6099.jpg.alt: Stacked plates of salt crust leading toward a magenta sunset over Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6099.jpg.story: I was back at the car with the bag packed when the light turned, and there is no version of that where you just drive away. Everything came out again. What made the unpacking worth it was the salt — those big stacked plates run in the same direction as the clouds, so the ground and the sky pull the eye the same way instead of fighting each other.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6099.jpg.location: Badwater Basin, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/death-valley/_DSC6135.jpg.title: Soft Geometry
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6135.jpg.alt: Low-contrast sunrise over the ridges of Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes, Death Valley National Park.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6135.jpg.story: Sunrise, but barely — the contrast never really arrived, and that turned out to be the mood worth keeping. One dune low in the frame, a second behind it, and a cloud above running the other way, so the eye zigzags up through the picture. There is almost no tonal separation anywhere in it. This one holds together on shape alone, which is rarer than good light.
/photos/death-valley/_DSC6135.jpg.location: Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes, Death Valley National Park, California

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6639.jpg.title: The Sheer Scale of It
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6639.jpg.alt: The Grand Canyon seen from Pima Point, a shaft of sunlight on red buttes above the distant Colorado River.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6639.jpg.story: This was one of the first scenes the Grand Canyon showed me. What pulled me in was a single streak of light raking across the buttes and reflecting off the Colorado far below. That warm rock against the cool, hazy blue was the shot.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6767.jpg.title: The Day's Last Ember
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6767.jpg.alt: The Grand Canyon at blue hour from Mojave Point, last light on the red buttes fading into cool twilight.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6767.jpg.story: Blue hour on my first evening in the canyon. I'd waited all day at Mojave Point for exactly this light - and then the last shuttle honked for me. I fired the shutter, ran over to ask the driver for two minutes to pack, and grabbed a few more frames while I had them. Each was an 8-second exposure at f/11, so every shot felt like forever in the fading light. I had no idea I'd just made one of my favorite Grand Canyon photographs.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6792.jpg.title: The Sentinel
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6792.jpg.alt: A lone juniper at the rim of the Grand Canyon at sunrise, first light striking the cliffs at Moran Point.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6792.jpg.story: I'd planned to shoot Lipan Point that morning, but I left too late - the sun was already breaking the horizon as I drove. Rather than gamble on making it, I pulled into the first overlook, Moran Point, and started hunting for a composition. Another photographer there was working a telephoto; I wanted to go wide. I found this lone juniper clinging to the edge and waited for the light to reach it.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6882.jpg.title: An Island of Light
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6882.jpg.alt: Sunlight on Berry Butte, rising from the hazy blue ridges of the Grand Canyon at Grandview Point.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6882.jpg.story: I was scouting a sunset composition at Grandview Point when streaks of light began falling across Berry Butte, while the ridges behind it dissolved into haze. The depth was already there - I just had to isolate it. I reached for 64mm to compress the layers and let the lit rock separate from the cool, hazy background. Sometimes the canyon hands you the shot; you just have to recognize it and frame it.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6909.jpg.title: Where the Sun Pours In
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6909.jpg.alt: A wide golden-hour view of the Grand Canyon from Grandview Point, the low sun glowing through haze above a dead tree.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6909.jpg.story: Once I'd found the right spot at Grandview Point, I wanted to keep it simple — a wide, near-panoramic frame with the low golden-hour sun pouring straight through the canyon. I used this lone dead tree to anchor the middle of the composition and shot into the light at 20mm, stopping down to f/11 so the sun held a clean shape. Some frames are less about a story and more about being there when the light is this good.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6976.jpg.title: Where Ridges Dissolve
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6976.jpg.alt: Layered ridgelines of the Grand Canyon fading into morning haze, with O'Neill Butte seen from Hopi Point at sunrise.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC6976.jpg.story: I stopped at Hopi Point on a morning hike to catch the sun coming up over O'Neill Butte. The light was doing the thing I love - stacking the ridgelines into receding layers as the haze separated each one. I reached for 77mm to compress those layers and let the butte sit as the anchor among them. It's a quiet, almost abstract way to photograph a place most people shoot wide.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7101.jpg.title: First light below the rim
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7101.jpg.alt: Warm morning light on a canyon wall seen from Coconino Overlook on the North Kaibab Trail
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7101.jpg.story: This was my first stop on the rim-to-rim journey I'd been wanting to do. I waited an hour for first light to come into the canyon as the clouds rolled in.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7356.jpg.title: Before the Sky Broke
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7356.jpg.alt: Wide-angle long-exposure view of Split Rock Falls, with storm clouds streaking across the sky above the canyon walls.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7356.jpg.story: After reaching Cottonwood Camp I doubled back toward the Manzanita rest area, where a small thunderstorm was rolling in. It felt like the perfect chance for a long exposure — something to play the falling water against the fast-moving clouds.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7356.jpg.location: Split Rock Falls, Grand Canyon, AZ

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7438.jpg.title: Desert's Garden
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7438.jpg.alt: A view from inside the alcove behind Ribbon Falls, a moss-covered rock in the foreground framed by the cave mouth.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7438.jpg.story: After a long day of hiking, I decided to visit Ribbon Falls. Getting the shot meant climbing up into a small alcove with all my gear, but it was worth it — sitting near the waterfall was refreshing on such a hot day. To handle the enormous dynamic range, from the shaded alcove to the bright canyon beyond, I blended two exposures together.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7592.jpg.title: Leaving the River Behind
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7592.jpg.alt: A barrel cactus in the foreground above the Colorado River, with the Black Bridge and soft evening light on the canyon walls.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7592.jpg.story: On my last evening in the canyon, I decided to photograph the Colorado River — this shot almost felt like the place saying goodbye to me. Once the light turned soft, I chose this barrel cactus to be the hero of the frame. To keep everything sharp from the spines at my feet to the bridge in the distance, I focus-stacked several frames together. Everything came together at once: the color in the river, the bridge, the light on the canyon walls, and its reflection in the water.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7696.jpg.title: An Older Rhythm of the Canyon
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7696.jpg.alt: Black-and-white photo of a mule pack train backlit by the rising sun on the South Kaibab Trail
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7696.jpg.story: While climbing back up to the South Rim, I had to stop and wait for a big mule train heading down to Phantom Ranch. I took the chance to photograph them against the canyon with the morning sun rising behind them. I shot straight into the low light and let the scene fall toward silhouette, working it in black and white so the long shadows became part of the frame.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7748.jpg.title: Light Letting Go
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7748.jpg.alt: Telephoto view of layered Grand Canyon ridgelines receding into golden sunset haze, seen from Desert View.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7748.jpg.story: On my last sunset in the park, I wanted to photograph the canyon from one of the South Rim's iconic spots, Desert View. I reached for my telephoto lens and found this almost abstract composition — the golden-hour light gradually giving out from the top of the frame to the bottom, the ridges flattening into one another the longer I looked.

/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7793.jpg.title: Purple Gold
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7793.jpg.alt: Wide view from Desert View, last light catching the far rim beneath a purple sky.
/photos/grand-canyon/_DSC7793.jpg.story: As the sun had almost disappeared, I caught this last light hitting the far rim and its final reflections on the Colorado River. I waited until the sun was nearly gone so the sky would shift into that band of purple above the warm rim. The purple-and-gold contrast, set against the green trees in the foreground, makes this one of my favorite shots from the whole Grand Canyon trip.

/photos/landscapes/_DSC0454-Edit.jpg.title: Lit from Within
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0454-Edit.jpg.alt: Mobius Arch in the Alabama Hills at night, its inner curve lit by headlamp, the Milky Way rising through the arch.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0454-Edit.jpg.story: I set the tripod low under the arch, then walked around behind it with the remote and a headlamp. One pass of light along the inner curve was all the arch needed — the rest of the frame I left to the Milky Way. Light painting is easy to overdo out here; I wanted the arch to look lit by something, not by me. One of my favourite astro frames.

/photos/landscapes/_DSC0500-Edit.jpg.title: Rain Check
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0500-Edit.jpg.alt: The Sentinel bristlecone pine at blue hour under streaked cloud, Schulman Grove, Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest, California.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0500-Edit.jpg.story: I came to Schulman Grove for an astro shot with this tree, and the weather had other plans — cloud rolled over the White Mountains and the stars never showed. So it became a blue-hour frame instead, with the yellow bloom at the base for a bit of colour against all that dead wood. I'm glad it went this way. It's the one bristlecone photo I have that doesn't look like everyone else's.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0500-Edit.jpg.location: Schulman Grove, Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest, California

/photos/landscapes/_DSC0540-Edit.jpg.title: Morrison and Laurel
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0540-Edit.jpg.alt: Convict Lake at midnight under the Milky Way, Mount Morrison and Laurel Mountain lit by long exposure, California.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0540-Edit.jpg.story: About five hours on the shore of Convict Lake for one frame. It's a time blend: a 900-second exposure to pull enough light onto Mount Morrison and Laurel Mountain, and a 20-second one for the sky so the stars stay as points instead of trails. Neither works alone at midnight — the long one smears the sky, the short one leaves the mountains black. Together they're close to what the eye almost saw.

/photos/landscapes/_DSC0671-HDR-Edit.jpg.title: August Steam
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0671-HDR-Edit.jpg.alt: Hot Creek winding through its gorge, faint steam over the water and morning light on Mammoth Mountain, California.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0671-HDR-Edit.jpg.story: August mornings at Hot Creek are warm, but the water is hot enough that it still steams at sunrise, and that steam was the whole plan. I wanted the vents smoking in the bends of the creek while first light landed on Mammoth Mountain behind them, so I was on the rim above the creek before the sun cleared the ridge. The window is short — as soon as the air warms up, the steam thins to nothing.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0671-HDR-Edit.jpg.location: Hot Creek Geological Site, Mammoth Lakes, California

/photos/landscapes/_DSC0801-Edit-2.jpg.title: Rothko's Mono Lake
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0801-Edit-2.jpg.alt: A lone tufa tower in Mono Lake under stacked storm clouds, water, hills and sky in flat bands of blue and grey, California.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0801-Edit-2.jpg.story: Midday at Mono Lake, a storm building over the far shore. I had come to scout compositions for the evening and this was the only frame I made all afternoon: lake, hills and cloud deck stacking into flat bands, and one tufa to give the eye somewhere to land. The long lens is the point — at 150mm the distance collapses and the layers sit on top of each other like colour fields. The name was obvious once I saw it on the back of the camera.

/photos/landscapes/_DSC0833-Edit.jpg.title: Sage and Storm
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0833-Edit.jpg.alt: Williams Butte and the Eastern Sierra at blue hour under storm clouds, sagebrush in the foreground, Lee Vining, California.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0833-Edit.jpg.story: A rare rainy day in a hot August, and the clouds it left behind were the reason to stop. I pulled off 395 near Williams Butte, on the way to Mono Lake, set the tripod among the sagebrush and waited for the last of the light while the cloud moved in over the mountains. Blue hour did the colour; the bushes hold the bottom of the frame so the sky can take up the rest.

/photos/landscapes/_DSC0844-Edit.jpg.title: Low Drama
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0844-Edit.jpg.alt: Tufa towers on the shore of Mono Lake at South Tufa in soft light before golden hour, calm water and thin cloud, California.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0844-Edit.jpg.story: Most tufa photos go for drama — sunset fire, Milky Way, storm light. This one is the opposite on purpose. I walked South Tufa in the hour before golden hour looking for a composition that felt calm: the towers standing in flat water, soft light, nothing shouting. It's the quiet frame in a set of loud ones, and this shore rewards that as much as it rewards the spectacle.

/photos/landscapes/_DSC0874-Edit.jpg.title: High Water
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0874-Edit.jpg.alt: Tufa towers reflected in Mono Lake at golden hour, receding storm clouds lit warm over South Tufa, California.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0874-Edit.jpg.story: After several days of rain the lake had come up noticeably, and water was standing among tufa that usually sits on dry ground. That's what made this frame — I wedged the camera and tripod under the tufa tower to get the towers reflected in water that isn't normally there. The clouds were the tail end of a long rainy day, pulling back and catching the last of the light. They gave the sky its balance: warm on top, warm in the reflection, and I didn't have to do anything but wait.

/photos/landscapes/_DSC0951-Edit.jpg.title: Perseid Night
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0951-Edit.jpg.alt: The Milky Way over the tufa towers of South Tufa, Mono Lake, during the Perseid meteor shower, reflected in still water.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC0951-Edit.jpg.story: South Tufa during the Perseids. I put the camera behind one of the big tufa formations with the tripod legs standing in the lake — the reflection needed the lens at water level. It was too dark for one exposure to carry both halves: the tufa is a 480-second exposure, the sky a 20-second one to keep the stars sharp, blended afterwards. Long night, and the Milky Way lined up exactly where I hoped.

/photos/landscapes/_DSC8109-Edit.jpg.title: Light in the Hollow
/photos/landscapes/_DSC8109-Edit.jpg.alt: Early-morning light streaming through the sea cave at El Matador Beach, god rays catching in the fog above a low-tide shoreline.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC8109-Edit.jpg.story: I planned this around the conditions — a low tide to expose El Matador's famous sea cave, and fog so the first light would hang in the air as visible streaks. The dynamic range was brutal, the bright cave mouth against the dark rock, so I blended two exposures to hold it all.
/photos/landscapes/_DSC8109-Edit.jpg.location: El Matador State Beach, Malibu, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8357-Edit.jp.title: Her Last Mile
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8357-Edit.jp.alt: Black and white photo of a lone hiker on the steep cinder slope of Cinder Cone, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8357-Edit.jp.story: She stopped to talk to my girlfriend and me while I was setting up for sunset — her last day in the park, Lassen Peak the day before. Then she walked on and became the thing the frame had been missing: something to hold that slope to scale. The conversion to black and white came later. Colour was doing nothing here that the shape of the cone wasn't already doing better.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8357-Edit.jp.location: Cinder Cone, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8392.jpg.title: Black Grit
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8392.jpg.alt: Black and white view across the crater rim of Cinder Cone, its cinder slopes curving away, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8392.jpg.story: The first volcano I ever climbed. Neither of us had seen anything like it — a cone of loose black grit with a crater bitten out of the top, and a trail that takes back half a step for every one you give it. I photographed the rim as geometry rather than as a place, and pulled the colour out afterwards. There was hardly any there to lose.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8392.jpg.location: Cinder Cone, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8413-Edit.jp.title: The Lone Guardian
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8413-Edit.jp.alt: A lone pine on the oxidised orange and black ash of the Painted Dunes at sunset, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8413-Edit.jp.story: I gave this an entire evening. The dunes only separate into bands when the sun is low enough to rake across them, and the window where the light held on this one tree — and not on the fifty others around it — lasted about two minutes. The rest of the evening was spent standing still, working out where I needed to be when it happened.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8413-Edit.jp.location: Painted Dunes, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8450-Edit.jp.title: Moon Over Sunrise
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8450-Edit.jp.alt: Full moon rising over Sunrise Peak at twilight, seen from the cinder slopes of Cinder Cone, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8450-Edit.jp.story: Entirely unplanned. We were already walking back down when the moon came up over Sunrise Peak, and I have never unpacked a tripod that fast — a full moon climbs a ridgeline quicker than feels reasonable, and every second of fumbling costs you the alignment. A single exposure: the twilight was still bright enough to hold the land and the moon in one frame.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8450-Edit.jp.location: Cinder Cone, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8632-HDR-Edi.title: Steel Clouds
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8632-HDR-Edi.alt: Kings Creek winding through a wildflower meadow below Reading Peak under heavy storm cloud, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8632-HDR-Edi.story: This was meant to be a scouting drive, but those steel-coloured clouds were not going to wait for a better-planned day. The composition needed the camera low and close to the bend, which meant standing in snowmelt at 14mm — cold enough that I stopped feeling my feet. Six stops of ND took it to a tenth of a second: enough to smooth the current without erasing it.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8632-HDR-Edi.location: Kings Creek Meadow, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8756-Edit.jp.title: Twilight Ghost
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8756-Edit.jp.alt: Full moon beside alpenglow on Lassen Peak, reflected in the still water of Manzanita Lake, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8756-Edit.jp.story: Four or five hours at this lake, shooting from golden hour through to full dark. The last hour was the hard part — cold, both of us ready to leave, waiting on the moon to clear Lassen Peak. The real obstacle was ducks. The lake was full of them, and a reflection like this needs a stretch of genuinely undisturbed water. Blended from two frames taken minutes apart.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8756-Edit.jp.location: Manzanita Lake, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8791-Edit.jp.title: Alien Grounds
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8791-Edit.jp.alt: Turquoise and milky-white hydrothermal pools and a dark mud pot in the crust at Bumpass Hell, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8791-Edit.jp.story: My first time anywhere like this. The smell reaches you before the view does, and then the colours arrive all at once — turquoise, rust, chalk-white, all within a few feet of each other. I didn't want a picture that explained where it was. I wanted the version that reads like a surface photographed from orbit, so I framed out the sky, the boardwalk and every other clue to scale.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8791-Edit.jp.location: Bumpass Hell, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8970-Edit.jp.title: Through the Trunks
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8970-Edit.jp.alt: Sunrise light on Manzanita Lake seen through pine trunks from the campground, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8970-Edit.jp.story: I was walking in to camp when I caught the light coming off the water between the trunks, with insects working in it further out. It is a photograph about backlight and nothing else — the trees are only there to break the glare into something the eye can rest on. I shot it from where I was standing. Stepping forward would have closed the gaps and cost me the whole thing.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC8970-Edit.jp.location: Manzanita Lake, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC9002-HDR-Edi.title: Sunrise in Hell
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC9002-HDR-Edi.alt: Sunrise light catching steam from the fumaroles of Bumpass Hell, framed by mountain hemlock, Lassen Volcanic National Park.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC9002-HDR-Edi.story: I scouted this the previous day and came back for it early. Cold air is the whole trick — the colder the morning, the more the vents give you, and at sunrise there was several times the steam I had seen in the middle of the day. The hemlocks were the other half of it. Without something solid in the corners, steam has nothing to be measured against.
/photos/lassen-volcanic/_DSC9002-HDR-Edi.location: Bumpass Hell, Lassen Volcanic National Park, California

/photos/people/81dJdwzh6qQ.jpg.title: The Calm in the Glare
/photos/people/81dJdwzh6qQ.jpg.alt: studio portrait, foil backdrop, colored lighting, fashion portrait, Izhevsk
/photos/people/81dJdwzh6qQ.jpg.story: I made this studio portrait of a friend in Izhevsk, Russia. The whole image is built on contrast — colored light raking across both her face and the crumpled foil behind her, and her smooth skin set against the hard, wrinkled metal. I gelled the lights warm and magenta so the foil would catch and throw color rather than sit flat.

/photos/yosemite/_AC16640-HDR.jpg.title: March Melt
/photos/yosemite/_AC16640-HDR.jpg.alt: Snowmelt surging over granite on the Merced River below Nevada Fall in March, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/yosemite/_AC16640-HDR.jpg.story: March, and the Merced was carrying everything the snowpack could give it. Getting down to this stretch below Nevada Fall was the awkward part — the trail is not built for stopping where I wanted to stop. Worth it, though. At full melt the river does things it does not do for the rest of the year, and there is no substitute for standing level with it.
/photos/yosemite/_AC16640-HDR.jpg.location: Nevada Fall, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/yosemite/_AC16669.jpg.title: Untamed
/photos/yosemite/_AC16669.jpg.alt: Nevada Fall in March seen looking downstream, heavy current below low cloud on the canyon walls, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/yosemite/_AC16669.jpg.story: Shot looking downstream from Nevada Fall rather than up at it — the less obvious direction, and the more violent one. The current in March is genuinely aggressive, and the cloud was sitting low enough on the walls to close the frame in on itself. I wanted this to feel untamed rather than scenic, so nothing here is soft: no clean horizon, no tidy light.
/photos/yosemite/_AC16669.jpg.location: Nevada Fall, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/yosemite/_AC16711.jpg.title: White Noise
/photos/yosemite/_AC16711.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of Yosemite Falls in full March flow pouring over granite, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/yosemite/_AC16711.jpg.story: Yosemite Falls in March, pushing through more water than the granite looks built for. I converted this one because colour was actively unhelpful — the scene is a grey cliff, white water and dark wet rock, and in colour that reads as a muddy version of itself. In monochrome it becomes a picture about shape and about the direction the water is travelling.
/photos/yosemite/_AC16711.jpg.location: Yosemite Falls, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/yosemite/_DSC9228.jpg.title: The Fisherman
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9228.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of a distant fisherman standing in the Merced River below granite peaks, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9228.jpg.story: Ninety-six millimetres, because he was a long way off and I wanted that distance compressed rather than described — anything wider and he would have been a speck in a lot of empty river. He is hard to find at first, which is deliberate. Once you have him the frame reorganises around him, and he becomes the only reliable indication of how big any of this is.
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9228.jpg.location: Merced River, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/yosemite/_DSC9410.jpg.title: His Spot
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9410.jpg.alt: Black and white photo of a tent on the granite summit of Clouds Rest above Yosemite Valley, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9410.jpg.story: I asked the hikers how they had settled on this spot. One of them told me he had camped up here twenty times and that it was 'his spot' — a very funny thing to hear said about the summit of Clouds Rest. I framed it with the drop behind rather than the sky, so the tent reads as perched rather than merely pitched.
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9410.jpg.location: Clouds Rest, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/yosemite/_DSC9497-HDR-Edit-2.jpg.title: Dawn on Tresidder
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9497-HDR-Edit-2.jpg.alt: Sunrise light on Tresidder Peak seen from the summit of Clouds Rest, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9497-HDR-Edit-2.jpg.story: Sunrise from the top of Clouds Rest, looking across at Tresidder Peak. This one is an exposure stack — the range was taking first light while everything below it was still holding night, and no single frame covers that spread without surrendering one end or the other. Stacked, the peak keeps its colour and the forest underneath keeps detail instead of falling to black.
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9497-HDR-Edit-2.jpg.location: Clouds Rest, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/yosemite/_DSC9604-HDR-Edit.jpg.title: Above the Fall
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9604-HDR-Edit.jpg.alt: The Merced River winding below heavy grey cloud above Nevada Fall near Little Yosemite Valley, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9604-HDR-Edit.jpg.story: The Merced a little way above Nevada Fall, near the Little Yosemite Valley camp. The cloud had gone flat and metallic, which is normally a reason to put the camera away. Here it was the whole point — river, fall, trees and sky all landed within about a stop of each other, so the picture holds on arrangement rather than on contrast between any of them.
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9604-HDR-Edit.jpg.location: Little Yosemite Valley, Yosemite National Park, California

/photos/yosemite/_DSC9663-HDR-Edit.jpg.title: Below the Bridge
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9663-HDR-Edit.jpg.alt: The Vernal Fall footbridge seen from a rock below it, the Merced River filling the foreground, Yosemite National Park.
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9663-HDR-Edit.jpg.story: The classic view of the Vernal Fall footbridge, which means the only decision left to make is where to stand. I worked down onto a rock slightly below bridge level. From there the water fills the bottom of the frame instead of draining out of it, and the bridge sits high enough to read as something people cross rather than as a line ruled across the picture.
/photos/yosemite/_DSC9663-HDR-Edit.jpg.location: Vernal Fall, Yosemite National Park, California
